utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you. Mr. Oric, good morning to you. Can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Gentlemen, yes, I can follow the proceedings in my mother tongue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And you may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours and also good morning to my learned friends of the Defence. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. I'm here together with co-counsel, Ms. Patricia Sellers, Mr. Gramsci di Fazio, Ms. Joanne Richardson and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you and your team, Mr. Wubben. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I am Vasvija Vidovic. Together with Mr. John Jones, we represent Mr. Naser Oric, and we have our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts with us. Good morning to my colleagues from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic, and good morning to you and your team. Any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, there is just one, Your Honour. We have been served with some documents which the Prosecution intends to use with this witness; I believe they intend to use it today as exhibits. I don't know if Your Honours have been served with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am not aware of them anyway, so I have yesterday's list.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, in any event, I have a submission to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or at least they may be listed here but I don't have a hard copy of it, in other words. I speak for myself. I don't know if my colleagues have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What I have in mind is ERN number 02115744, 02115781, I believe. Anyway, there's a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, they are listed. They are listed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. It's simply this: That firstly, obviously, Racine Manas hasn't given any evidence about the provenance of these documents. There is no indication on any of the documents of the collection or the source from which they came. There are no -- we have no seizure details. There are no signatures as far as I can see. They are mostly undated or some are dated from 1995 or later, and there are names of Serb places like Han Pijesak, places which were in Serb hands at the relevant time, Han Pijesak, Bratunac. And it's simply this: That in these circumstances, we -- sorry, my apologies. Sorry, these submissions also cover yesterday's documents, which were the lists of fighters from Osmace, purportedly from Osmace. And it's simply this: That it could be that, you know, for all we know someone yesterday or a year ago or two years ago sat down with a list of names and typed up some documents and filled in some details of weaponry and whatnot. And we are well aware that the approach of the Tribunal is to basically put everything in the kitchen sink and then at the end of the trial see what weight you give to it. But, in our submission, there has to be some limit, and in these circumstances where we really -- these are in our submission nothing more than scraps of paper which anyone could have composed at any given time. To put it before the witness, firstly, with any suggestion that they have any probative value may mislead the witness firstly, so I would certainly, if these documents are used, object to it being suggested in any way to the witness that he should think that these are in any way of any probative value, that they are authentic or anything. On the one hand, I know that when the witness is present, we are not meant to say, well, we are not meant to make vocal our concerns about authenticity, but conversely if must be the case that the Prosecution can't suggest that these actually have any authenticity or any authentic value, especially when they are undated, unsigned, and we have got no idea where they came from. But I would also actually submit that if the Prosecution uses these documents and applies for them to be exhibits that this is the sort of thing which actually should be excluded and declared inadmissible, unless there are some details about where these documents came from. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you think there is anything on the face of it which would render them inadmissible straight away?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Depends on what criteria the Chamber is applying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because, for example, I will just mention one thing with regard to the last document. I'm sorry I'm giving you my back, Judge Eser. But with regard to the last document that -- okay. He's seeing me there. That had the supposedly the list of the 121 members of the A3 unit of the Osmace territorial force. I'm just saying alleged to be so. I mean, it's -- your witness did recognise the names. So let's put it like this. I mean, fortunately, in such a matter we speak the same language, for sure, and we speak it in the most clear terms, that this is a Prosecution document, exhibit, and it rests entirely with the Prosecution to prove first the authenticity of the document and the probative value in any case of the document because the document can be authentic but also be -- contain false information and whatever. So that is something that rests with the Prosecution until the very end. I do appreciate of course you raising up the matter because I agree with you that these are not signed, these are not stamped, these -- and we have got no idea at all about provenance. The same applies, although not to that extent, to one of the documents you made use of during the examination-in-chief. I was leaving it until the very end. I would like to know from the Prosecution because it's obviously a document that has been provided to you by the Prosecution because it has an ERN number, because -- I would like to know whether -- what the provenance of the document. I will point it out later on. But again, where definitely Mr. Jones is 100 per cent right, is that you have a number of documents, some of which you have made use of, some of which you purportedly intend to make use of. We have no clue as to the provenance of these documents. At least, you should provide us with that much of information so that we would also be able to weigh as we go along the probative value that you are attributing to this or these documents because you're making use of them by showing them to a witness and asking the witness to give his comments on these documents. It cuts both ways. I mean, I don't need to explain why it cuts both ways but it does cut both ways. But I think you do owe us and the Defence at least information on the provenance. Now, whether these were actually typed later on, whether they are invented, et cetera, for the time being it's a proposition that is forthcoming from the Defence. It could be something that can result ultimately to be true. It can be just sheer, pure imagination or conjecture. But at this point in time, you're right. At this point in time, you're right to express this concern because they are unsigned and unstamped, and we don't know what the provenance is, so at least we should know what the provenance is. I will of course, for the time being, while this is being explored by your case manager, or by whoever, I mean, I'm saying the case manager, I don't know whether it's her role or not, I will ask you to proceed with the cross-examination and make use of these, because I trust the Prosecution enough to think that they will be coming forward and tell us what the provenance is. I don't think the provenance is the Office of the Prosecution, so -- for a moment I don't even suspect that for a moment. So I am going to allow them to make use of these. Obviously, if as we go along, nothing materialises, then we will come back to the matter. But I think this is something that can be verified without any major problems. I thank you for raising the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour, and obviously I don't wish to draw it out. It was simply to get our concerns on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. If it was a futile or an uncalled for comment I would have brushed it aside in my own style and you know that I can do that. It's certainly not the kind of comment that would be better brushed aside.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It calls for some action from --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour. And just to add that when I put forward the possibility that these might have been forged or equally in the context of the interview of the accused that it might not have been conducted properly, these aren't conjectures which I obviously intend to prove. I'm raising them in the spirit that the Prosecution has to satisfy -- that that isn't the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course you don't need to explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, thank you. I understand everything that's transpired, and I understand Mr. Jones's concerns. Just for the Defence, for the sake of today's proceedings, the only other list that I intend to use is that which I'll call the A4 Biljeg list which is 02115703 through to 5711, so that's the only other one. I know of they've got more, but I'm just putting them on notice so that they understand that that's the only one that I'm going to use today. The second issue is this: Yes, we can provide you with the limited evidence that we have regarding provenance. And that would have -- I can't give evidence from the bar table obviously, but I could if the Defence so wish, or if the Trial Chamber so wish, eventually provide you with MIFS and tender them into evidence which would -- you know what the MIFS and the IFS are. So that would be at this stage of the proceedings the only evidence that we can provide to you, and of course we are more than willing to do so. I would simply be handing it up from the bar table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, let me make myself clear. Our priority at this point in time is to finish with this witness. That's why I said you will proceed with making use of whatever documents you intended to make use of in the first place. Then we are expecting once the matter has been raised to provide us with all due information on provenance. All right? Now, whether it should be sworn evidence or not, that can be attended to at a later stage but it should not take any of our time of today. That's -- I think I've made myself clear there. MR. DI FAZIO: Crystal clear, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Now it's 9.18. How much of today's time do you think you will need to finish your cross-examination? MR. DI FAZIO: The lion's share of the day. I'm going to need a lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Because I would take it that there is going to be a re-examination. We have got some questions of our own.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, five or ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Five or ten minutes. Okay. MR. DI FAZIO: I'll adjust accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's say leave the last half an hour for us. MR. DI FAZIO: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It could be 20 minutes. Even if we need to go a little bit beyond, I don't think there is anyone sitting in this courtroom in the afternoon. I would just ask for the usual indulgence. I always find the cooperation of everyone, provided it doesn't go beyond a few minutes. So let's bring the witness in. I meant to discuss -- do you have a quick response, Mr. Wubben, to the motion regarding D002? If it's yes or no only for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you plan to agree to the request, would you let Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. us know today, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: We will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Buric, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome back. I hope you had a good rest. We were discussing and see how best to try and make sure that we finish with you today so that you can go back home because you've been here for quite a long time already. So please take a seat. Make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, once more I remind you that you are testifying under oath or in terms of the solemn declaration that you entered last week. Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Buric, just a very brief reminder from me. If you can . Please answers questions with a yes or no if you possibly can, and please keep your answers short and that way we will whip through the remainder of this cross-examination, God willing. Now, yesterday we were talking about some -- the Osmace grouping of men that you've spoken about. And I showed you a list. I want to show you another list now. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, it's document bearing ERN number 02115703 through to 5711. And while we are there, could the witness also have P80, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, okay. Do you have a -- I think you have a copy in -- of the document. I see you nodding. I take that to be yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. I want a confirmation of that. Mr. Buric, you have been given this document in your own language, the first page starts with 02115703. Do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, yes, Mr. Di Fazio. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The document on the face of it seems to speak for itself. It's a list of members of the unit A4 from Biljeg, and number 1 on the list is this gentleman Ahmo Tihic who you've already spoken about. And it says that he was born in Lijesce. Do you see that entry, number 1, entry number 1?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Ahmo Tihic, was he born in Lijesce, as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Now, what I'd like you to do is exactly the same exercise as we conducted with that other document that I showed you. Just go through, cast your eye down the lists - I'll give you time - and go through it, and look at the names and tell us if any of those names are names that you can associate with any grouping, any self-organised grouping of men in or from the Biljeg area.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this list, I know some lads from that area, from Miholjevina, Mocici, Delici, Mehmedovici. In my opening statement I said that Biljeg was a wooded, forested area where there was a lot of refugees from Skelani, Lijesce, Zanjevo, from those villages that had been expelled in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Thanks. Now, if you go through the list, you'll find that -- firstly, do you see that number, that printed number at the top right-hand corner of each page? You see that number? That computer number? Top, right-hand corner, 02115703. Do you see that? Yes, I should be glad if you could point it out.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Thanks. If you flick through to the last page of this document with a number ending 5711, it's different from the preceding pages in that it bears the number or designation A4/1. You see that?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Right. Okay. Now on that particular page, the numbering of the people is different because it starts at number 1 and finishes at 9. Now, I'll be absolutely clear with you. If you add up those numbers, 127 from the preceding page plus 9 is -- adds up to about -- adds up not to about, but to 136 conscripts or, sorry, 136 people. Okay? And if you also look now at the paragraph 4 of the TO Biljeg in document P80, which I think you have there, that also refers to two companies, A4 and A4/1 consisting of 136 conscripts under the commander Ahmo Tihic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Okay. You, I -- I'm sure Mr. Jones will correct me if I'm wrong but I think this was a P80. I think P80 was the document that you described as a work of fantasy. Bearing in mind what I've just shown you, this new document with the list of 136 people bearing A4 and A4/1 designation, are you prepared to reconsider your evidence that P80 is a work of fantasy or do you remain of that opinion?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by my statement that this is just pure fiction. What you showed me has no date. I know most of the lads, well, I know some of the lads from this list. And it's like I said before, this is a list of the population who happened to be in refuge from that area, from the villages of Mocici and some other villages. This list was made after the relevant time. It was probably during the demilitarised period and does not represent the actual state of affairs on the ground at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. To be fair to you, do you -- are you just speculating that it was made after the demilitarisation, or is it the case that you just don't actually know. You've got no idea when this document was created? I'm not talking about P4. I'm talking about the Biljeg document that I've just put to you.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I state with a great deal of certainty that this document was drafted later because there were no lists, records, reviews or I don't even know what to say, made in Srebrenica until the demilitarisation. Not one single piece of paper was there to see in the Srebrenica area before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thanks. Could you just -- MR. DI FAZIO: Could Your Honours just bear with me for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: These lists that I've shown you, the one I've got just in front of you -- the one you've got just in front of you now with Biljeg A4 and the other list that I showed you yesterday in relation to Osmace, the names that you saw on those lists of the men and the names that you're currently looking at, aren't they all fighters who were part of the self-organised groupings in Osmace, at some point or another, or Biljeg? You see, there is no women listed here, for example. So is my -- am I correct in that?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I said, this is a census, a list of people ranging in age from 16 to 60. These are not members of units or armed groups. I state with a great deal of certainty that this is a list of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Well, just look at the document that you've got in front of you now. One of the -- right. The column, there's three columns and then you can see the date of birth, okay? Look at the first page. A good number of them, of these men, are aged -- well, were born in the early 1960s and early 1970s, just on that first page with the exception of Mr. Ahmo Tihic. He's not doing too badly; he was born in 1955. So they are not old men there, are they? Older men, I should say. And if you cast your eye -- in fact, if you cast your eye over the next page you've got fellows born in the 1960s, the early 1970s. In fact, if you cast your eye over into the third page the oldest one there was born in 1956. Sorry, I apologise, I mislead you. There was one there born in 1946. Number 37. Do you see him? 37 and 48. They are the two oldest gentlemen on that page from what I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There is a 1945. MR. DI FAZIO: There we go, 1945, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So number 47. Those three are the oldest on that particular page. And I think, if you turn over on to page bearing the number 5706, again you will see that the majority of them were born in the 1960s and 1970s with the exception of number 60, Ismet Hodzic, who was born in 1940. Which makes him about 52 during the war, right? So my point is that these are all, the vast majority of these names here are the names of younger men, men who would be quite capable of fighting. Would you agree with that? Sorry, what's your answer? Do you agree with me that the vast majority are younger men who were quite capable of fighting?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It states so here in the list but that doesn't have to be so out in the field, and it was not a rule for men to join a certain group and to take part in combat activities. There were 30.000 people of this age in Srebrenica. Had they all been soldiers, then we would have been well. There were over 30.000 people born in this range of years in Srebrenica at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, just to make sure, because -- in page 5709, number 97 and number 101, Bahrija Barakovic, Efendija Memic, are those males or females? Is the name Bahrija the name of a man or of a woman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Depending on the accent, Bahrija can be the name of a woman or a man. And the second person is Efendija, that's a man. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What about number 109, Nurija, Nurija Salihovic?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's also a man's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Anyway, but your position is that there is -- that these are just names, it's just a census and it's not -- there is no characteristic about the names that you've seen here that tends to indicate to you that this is a list or a grouping of young men capable of fighting in 1992, the majority of them anyway?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that these lists were drafted at some point in the demilitarised zone. There is no date and the lists do not reflect or refer to the situation out in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I tender the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This will become 5 --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 571, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will become document Exhibit -- Prosecution Exhibit P571. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. I -- just one quick question with respect to P75, if I could ask the witness briefly to look at that. I have just one very simple question in relation to P75. Well, actually two or three. You were shown this document by Mr. Jones, and he took you to some of the content of it, and asked you some details about the personalities mentioned here. First one he mentioned was Nedzad Bektic from Karacici. And he asked you if it is true, as it says in this document, that he was an organiser of armed resistance in the area of Kragljivoda, and you said no, the organiser of resistance in the Kragljivoda group was Sefik Mandzic. I don't think I need show you but do you know that book that I showed you yesterday, the book that is apparently on the face of it written by Mr. Naser Oric, if in that book it were to be claimed that Mr. Bektic led the Kragljivoda unit, would that sway you? Would that change your opinion about P75 in any respect?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I state with a great deal of certainty that the organiser of the resistance in Kragljivoda is Sefik Mandzic. Bektic Mandzic at the time, as a military cadet, was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And one of the -- one of the other reasons for -- as I read your -- understand your evidence for you casting doubt on P75 is that the fellow Atif Krdzic is described as being from Srebrenica, and I think the thrust of your evidence was that he just had no connection with Srebrenica because he had a house -- he had a house in Bratunac and he was from Osmace. Did he ever --

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did he ever live in Srebrenica at all, spend time there?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't live in Srebrenica. He lived at Osmace and in Bratunac. He had two houses, in Osmace and Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What was his occupation before the war?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He worked as an active police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Srebrenica. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank. I've finished with P75. Sorry, if Your Honours just bear with me I might be able to draw some lines through my notes. All right. I now want to show you another document. I just remind you of your general evidence. There is no army in existence in the Srebrenica area throughout 1992, no BiH army. That's correct, isn't it? No command structures, no organisation of any sort at all, apart from the self-organised, small self-organised group. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. Yes. Just want to show you this document. I'll be very brief with this document, Mr. Buric. I can take you straight to the part that I'm interested in. This document is just -- it's a decision granting a certain gentleman -- there is no need to mention his name incidentally. That's not important for our purposes, okay? Who has received some sort of assessment as -- that enables him to a disability pension, and it appears to be signed by you. Would you have a look at the document and tell us if that's correct.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked as a deputy chief for social security for war veterans and the disabled but this is not my signature. When I issued documents or dealt with the process of granting assistance, this was in the office, until the year 2005, but I don't think this -- this is definitely not my signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Just -- it seems -- Mr. Di Fazio, may I please -- and Madam Vidovic and Mr. Jones, please follow me carefully. This seems -- no, not seems -- this is obviously a photocopy of a document which you must have in your records. Now, it seems to me that in the photocopying process, the right-hand side of the script is not photocopied entirely. I think there is something missing from top to bottom. If you look at the very bottom of the -- MR. DI FAZIO: Last page, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, on the last page. If you look at the very end of that last page, I'm saying 00686335, right-hand corner, to the right of what you suggested could be the witness's signature and which he contests, there is something written which I suggest to you could be "za," and "za" means "for," so if you have the -- do you follow me or not? MR. DI FAZIO: I understand you, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it could provide the explanation for the whole matter, whether there is his signature or not. If it's -- because if it's -- be -- whatever signature Buric, Nesib or Hasib or whatever and "za," that would mean that it is "for" someone, put the name but it's -- and -- anyway, I don't know, perhaps you can trace the original, if you have it in your document, in your records, and it would show "za" if there is indeed "za." MR. DI FAZIO: I understand. And anyway, the witness has said it's not his signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if there is "za" it would strengthen the statement of the witness. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, I understand that and -- I understand, Your Honour, and I'll make every inquiry to see if the original sheds any light on that and if it does, then of course we will make it instantly clear to the Defence. So we will undertake to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. So it's not your signature --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Also, I find it strange that one -- in signing one's name you put the initial for your surname but then your entire first name. I mean, it's -- I take it that the family name of the witness is Buric, not Nesib. Why would one sign B full stop and then Nesib. MR. DI FAZIO: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, I can see Nesib on its own without a B and without the surname. I mean, that occurs in many cultures, but it's the first time in my life that I see the surname, the family name, being initialised only and the first name in full. I mean, but anyway it's up to you, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You say that's not your signature. Did someone else write, if you're aware, did someone else write your name there under the name "sekretar" where your name is printed?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Someone else conducted administrative procedure, and this is another person's signature. I signed quite a number of decisions but never in this to call it style because I signed in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: There is nothing -- having seen the document, forgetting about the signature, there is nothing -- would you agree with me it's a perfectly innocuous decision granting some chap a pension? Is there any reason for you to doubt the -- whoever wrote your name at the end of it, is there any reason for you to doubt that this is a genuine decision? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know this Kadric, Nedzad, and I don't know this document, and where it came from and what the intention was. The ministry that issues decisions concerning servicemen keep their records, and I don't know whether this handicapped person is a genuine person, who he was, where his file is kept, and I don't know what the intention of this document was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Right. Okay. Well, I think the intention was to give him a pension, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a pension. Pensions were approved by the ministry for veterans affairs and this concerns the aid for the disability.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Cut to the chase with the document. Look under statement of reasons, please. See that -- an application dated 23rd of April, the gentleman from Srebrenica requests to be recognised as a war disabled serviceman on the basis of the evidence provided and enclosed, the following has been established, that the above member was -- that the above was a member of the RBH army in Srebrenica, VJ, military unit, in the period from 10th of May, 1992, and that he was wounded on duty on the 13th of July, 1995. I've got a very simple question. If this document is true, if it really is a granting of a pension to -- or something, something to this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Disability allowance. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Disability allowance to this man, okay? If it truly is that, is there any particular reason why the municipal secretariat for the protection of disabled servicemen would consider that he was a member of a non-existent army from the 10th of May, 1992? Non-existent on the basis of course of what you said.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim with full responsibility that there was no army. This document was compiled in 1998, and I stated earlier that during the demilitarisation, on paper some structure was established concerning the operative group and the 28th Division. I wasn't there when they were putting together those documents, but prior to the demilitarisation there were no military units. There were only organised groups. And the way they structured it during the demilitarisation, I don't know how they went about it but they created the operations group and the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My objection was to the characterisation of this witness's testimony as being that there was no army of RBH and it was therefore a non-existent army. His evidence was clearly relating to Srebrenica if not Osmace. He's not saying there was never any -- as far as I heard his evidence, that the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina never existed. So long as that's clear. MR. DI FAZIO: No, that is clear, and that is the -- exactly what I intend to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I understood it throughout. And that's why I told to you wait because I -- I don't think that was ever an issue. MR. DI FAZIO: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Lines 10 to 11, a non-existent army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. Oh, yes, but I understood throughout yesterday when the questioning was taking place that we were talking of a particular, localised army, army unit, and not the army, the entire army of -- MR. DI FAZIO: I understand Mr. Jones --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we have documentary proof of that, when that came into being in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. MR. DI FAZIO: I seek to tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This will be 572, P572. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Buric, that's the end of documents for the time being. I want to ask you some questions about Fakovici. You gave detailed evidence that described the disposition of Serb forces, Serb units, in the Fakovici area, quite detailed information, including that Serb units were there from Bijeljina and the White Eagles were operating there. Do you remember that evidence?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that they received people from the units of Skelani, Bratunac and Bijeljina, with the help of the Serbs from Serbia proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you have that information before you went to Fakovici in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When did you acquire that information?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on we found some documents of theirs, diaries, agendas. When the civilians departed towards Fakovici, some of their documentation was found in various houses. And we all concluded that all what the units were that came to the area of Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Who collected these documents?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the farmers who went there to get food found some of their documents. They would write down where the aid came from, and it came from the areas I specified previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Who would write down things? The farmers? The farmers who went there to get food? Or are you saying the Serbs -- I withdraw that question. I'll withdraw it. What aid are you -- what aid are you talking about? Are you talking about military aid? Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. And the farmers who went there to get food, are they -- are they the civilians who went into these villages in search of food? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not farmers per se but people who lived in the surrounding villages who went to Fakovici to get food.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: If there is any problems with the transcript, I would like to be alerted now before I proceed any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when the witness was telling about the documents found in the Serb houses, he never said that anyone wrote anything down. It can be deducted from the transcript that the farmers were writing things down, but perhaps the witness could clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that definitely -- if that -- if Madam Vidovic is correct, in other words, if the witness never said that they wrote down -- MR. DI FAZIO: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me read out to the witness what I have in the transcript and the interpreters please make sure that this is interpreted verbatim to the witness. The witness is at page 22, line 11, he is, according to the transcript, reported as having answered to your question, who collected these documents, as follows: "Answer: I said that the farmers who went there to get food found some of their documents. They would write down where the aid came from and it came from the areas I specified previously." Now, I would rather prefer not to comment what that means, whether who wrote down whether it's the farmers or whoever wrote down -- wrote down those documents. First of all, did you -- does this reflect what you said? Or would you like to explain to us exactly what you meant and what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said the following: The farmers from the nearby villages who went to get food in Fakovici found some Serb papers. They found Serb papers and what was stated there was who was in that area, what units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That's how I had understood it in the first place. When I read the transcript, I didn't understand it as meaning that the witness had said that the farmers had written down these details. I had understood it that whoever had drafted those documents had written Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. down the sources of military aid. That's how I had understood it anyway. MR. DI FAZIO: And I'm grateful to Madam Vidovic for clarifying that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, same here. And I think you realised that when you withdrew your question, actually, I think. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, I think so

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So the farmers found the documents that gave information in -- presumably in Serb, Serb buildings, and what did they do with the documents thereafter?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what they did with the documentation, but I know that the first groups to arrive, the ones in Joseva and Jagodnja, these documents were shown, they were showed pieces of diaries, articles from newspapers, even proper documents, with specific units. When the Serbs withdrew from Fakovici, they left their documentation behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Well, but hang on. When did the farmers show you the documents? Because you said -- you said that the first groups, when they arrived Joseva and Jagodnja they were shown the documents, but the operation in Fakovici occurred after that, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said they were showing it to the guys from those villages, and they were never shown to me. I said that some information reached us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I see. So your evidence relating to military dispositions of Serb units or forces in that area is based on documents found by farmers in houses who related it to other soldiers from or fighters Joseva and Jagodnja, who in turn related it to you?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You asked me where did we get the information from as to what units were in Fakovici during the war, so I tried to explain where we got the documents from. These were Serb documents, and when Fakovici fell, people continued finding those documents in various houses for days. So we are talking about the period after Fakovici fell and we are talking about documents that were found in their houses, and they were taken to Jagodnja and Joseva, and these documents were being shown to the guys there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that such material showing the disposition of Serb forces, where they are located, what units were there, what types of units, were absolutely invaluable to these self-organised groups, absolutely crucial to have such information, because that would tell you where they were, what plans they had, what strengths they had? You would agree with that, wouldn't you? Crucial information. It's called intelligence in a more traditional warfare situation.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Why not? Why isn't it important to know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think -- I mean, certainly for my part I'm aware that there is a lag in interpretation. I can even hear it when it is still being interpreted. But the interpretation was still going when the witness said no, and then Mr. Di Fazio was in with his next question. It's not fair to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair comment, yes. So let's go through this. You said no. What did you say no for -- to? When you said no, what did you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I meant that we didn't have information prior to that. We didn't know where their positions and forces were. Those documents were found afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please repeat your question, then, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I understand what you've said. My question is about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: -- the use to be made of the documents after they had been found and after they have been shown to the self-organised groups of fighters. Would you agree with me that the information contained in such papers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait until -- wait until Mr. Di Fazio finishes his question and it has been fully interpreted to you before you answer, because then we can end up with a confused answer or a confused interpretation of your answer. Mr. Di Fazio, I'm -- I apologise to you for having interrupted you, cut you halfway but I noticed that the witness was again trying to answer when you were still in the process of finishing your question. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the information contained in these papers concerning the disposition of Serb forces was -- would be invaluable to self-organised groups such as your own and the others that you've mentioned? Absolutely invaluable.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The information we had came later when Fakovici fell, so such information meant nothing to us. We only learned what the units were before in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: But the Serb units remained in the area, didn't they? And it was important to know what type of units were operating in the area, what type of equipment they had. So I suggest to you that such information would have been almost as valuable as diamonds in that situation. What do you think?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Later on, we didn't move to those areas, only civilians to get food. When with we retreated around 3.00 or 4.00 in the afternoon, the armed Muslim groups never returned to that area again. We were not interested. Only civilians came in their search of food.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you preserve the documents and hand them on to any other armed groups in the area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the objection. He never said that he came in possession of these documents. In fact, he said that they were not even shown to him. MR. DI FAZIO: I'll withdraw my question. That's quite correct and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We're not letting you but I anticipated what the objection was going to be. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can I ask you this: Are you aware of the documents having been preserved and passed on to other groups?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Were there other occasions when you came across such documentation giving you information about the disposition of Serb forces in other locations? For example, in areas around Osmace or perhaps later in the Kravica area?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were none in the area of Osmace. And as for Kravica, that was the only time when I was there and I returned around 4.00 p.m. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You gave detailed information about the disposition of Serb forces in Kravica. How did you acquire that information?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in Kravica, but in the axis that we underdid the reconnaissance on which was Avdagina Njive.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed the other toponym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Could you repeat -- could you please repeat this last part of your answer? Not in Kravica, but in the axis that we underdid the reconnaissance on which was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, reconnaissance, Avdagina Njive-Kajici. That's what we saw in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So in Kravica, you had no documentary evidence to inform you as to what Serb forces you faced, what their disposition was?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My group from Osmace didn't have. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Let's leave this topic and move to another area of the Fakovici episode. You said that on the 4th of October, you and the grouping of self-organised fighters from Osmace went to assist in Kragljivoda and that you went to assist in defending against a powerful attack. Do you recall that evidence? This is before -- before you get to Fakovici, of course.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. How many of you went from your Osmace grouping?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Perhaps around 20 from my group.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. All of them armed?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. About ten of them had rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you see fighting in Kragljivoda? Or to be more precise, were you and your group involved in fighting, actually involved in fighting, in Kragljivoda?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was daily combat from Jezero and Vitez towards Kragljivoda. Artillery was used. Their APC was moving about, firing at the position of Kragljivoda.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Who made the decision to go from Osmace to Kragljivoda? If anyone.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one made that decision. If you have the written form in mind, whenever there was any danger, as soon someone would come to tell us that a certain area was under attack and since it was close as the crow flies, and when we could hear shooting, then we would go there, so we went towards Kragljivoda.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I just had a decision in mind, any sort of decision. Whether it was an oral decision or a written decision is not what I'm seeking. I just want to know who decided that the 20 men are going to go from Osmace to Kragljivoda to assist in this action. It might have been a committee, it might have been you, it might have been put to the vote. I don't know. It might have been in writing. I just want to know the mechanics of the decision. How was it arrived at?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there were always around ten guys in my group from the same village. It was a somewhat larger village of 70 or 80 houses, and we were there in the street, we assembled and went towards Kragljivoda.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. That's what happened. But who made the decision? Who made the decision? Did you all show your hands? Did you --

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said already it was me. No, no, there was no discussion. When you needed help, there were all volunteers. It was all on a voluntary basis. I proposed it, and about 20 lads who were around me agreed and we all immediately set off in the direction of Kragljivoda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I heard when the witness replied "I" and this did not get into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. What is still not clear -- I mean, I've been following your questions and his answers. You put a question -- let me take you back a little bit, at the previous page. You put a question, it was two questions in one actually, and this is what probably caused it. We are page 30 -- sorry, page 29, line 24, lines 24 to 25, and the first page on -- first line on page 30. Your question was the following: Did you see fighting in Kragljivoda? That was the first question. And then you continued: "Or to be more precise, were you and your group involved in fighting, actually involved in fighting?" And his answer at the time was: "Yes, there was daily combat from Jezero and Vitez towards Kragljivoda. Artillery was used. Their APC was moving about, firing at the position in Kragljivoda." Which to me seems more of an answer answering the question, did you see fighting in Kragljivoda? Since you started with that question, it probably was interpreted, did you see with your naked eyes fighting in Kragljivoda. And he missed completely the second part of the question, which was explanatory of the first part. And he never gave us a statement. He's explained that he went there. He decided to go there. He suggested to -- and he had volunteers to go there, but he's never actually stated that his group of 20 people, including himself, were actually involved in the fighting. I know what you asked in the first place, but the way it was interpreted must have misled him. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. So the question is: Did you actually get involved in fighting, firing your weapons, and so on, actual fighting?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Of course, at any point in time, the 20 or so men could have decided they didn't want to stay there, couldn't they?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We could have decided not to stay there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Well, not just we could have decided. Any individual or group of two or three, or four or five, or six or seven, or eight or nine out of that group of 20 could have decided at any moment that for good reason or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. for bad, that they just wouldn't want to stay there and fight, and go back to Osmace. That was always possible, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did that ever happen at all in 1992, with your Osmace group?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To leave the positions? This happened on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What did you do in that situation, in the midst of fighting?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can just give you one example.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When Kragljivoda was falling on the 20th or the 21st of March, 1993, I was at that position, and that's when food delivery action by parachutes began there. And I already talked about large columns of Serb artillery weapons going in the direction of Jezero, Vitez, Kragljivoda. And if you believe me, on the line where there was supposed to be about 50 men, there were about 11 who remained from that Kragljivoda group, 11 of them. When the line was falling, all the people left in order to look for food. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. So any military action that any self-organised grouping engaged in depended entirely on individual members of that self-organised grouping deciding to remain; correct? Or depended to a large extent on --

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything was on a voluntary basis. If they wanted to stay, they stayed. If they did not want to stay, they would go.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Now, turning to the next day, I think you said that civilians from Joseva and Jagodnja came to Kragljivoda on the morning of the 5th. Do you remember that? Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you still engaged in fighting in Kragljivoda? You and the Osmace grouping, self-organised grouping?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were there and when we saw the first civilians going into the villages of Gladovici and Sljivica, we decided to go and see what they had set on fire there. On the 5th in the morning. We decided, Sefik and I, to go to Joseva and Jagodnja to see what had been burnt and what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: My question is: On the morning that the civilians from Jagodnja and Joseva arrived, were you still engaged in fighting in Kragljivoda? Were you still engaged in actual combat there?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a line from Kragljivoda, from Vitez to Kragljivoda. In the morning, the infantry fire was weaker. The Serbs were just shelling the positions intensely. When they would go to one side, they would compensate by shelling on a different side. So that that side would receive aid. So there was active shelling. That's what happened that morning with Kragljivoda.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So you became aware of the civilians coming down from Joseva and Jagodnja. You and Sefik went to another village, and do I understand you correctly, you spoke to them there about what was happening further north in -- further north-east in Jagodnja and Joseva?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We went in that direction where the village was burned, the Joseva and Jagodnja villages. We went in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And who made the decision at that point to move the Osmace grouping from that area to -- up to Jagodnja and Joseva?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my decision. I said that we should go there to see what was going on, and the majority of the group accepted this, and they went with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You weren't -- I want to understand you clearly. Did you just say that you went up there to see what was going on?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: That's the reason that you went there, to see what was going on?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim villages were burning. Civilians were killed. We went to help people. We didn't go for a picnic. We went to help the Muslim villages. Joseva, Jagodnja were burning. The Serbs made an incursion there on the 5th, and people were getting killed, houses were burning. We went there to help people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And just to -- so we are absolutely clear about the reason that you moved from the Osmace area up to Jagodnja and Joseva, I just want to put some evidence to you before the break. You were asked by Mr. Jones on the 9th of September, page 3, this is the question: "When we left off yesterday, you were describing how, I think it was on the morning of the 5th of October 1992, and correct me if I misstate any of this, you and Sefik Mandzic and your men set off for Joseva and Jagodnja because you heard those villages were attacked and on fire. Is that a correct summary of what you're telling us?" Answer: "Yes." And question: "Just for the transcript, and again I think you stated yesterday but specifically that those villages had been attacked by Serbs in Fakovici. That's what you told us." Answer: "Yes."

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in Fakovici, but from Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. And later, when he was asking you about the captured civilians, Mr. Jones sought further clarification. "Let me approach it this way. You set off with Sefik Mandzic and his group to Joseva and Jagodnja. Part of your information was that Muslim civilians had been taken captive. Was it any part of your intention to -- or not it try and rescue or liberate those captives?" Answer: "We came to help. Our intention was to assist the Muslim villages, Jagodnja and Joseva, to defend themselves against the attack, for the villages not to be set on fire. In Joseva and Jagodnja, there were refugees from various places. So our primary intention was to defend that Muslim village, those two Muslim villages, Jagodnja and Joseva." You agree with that. Firstly, you said that and you agree now, don't you, that that was your intention, okay?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Your intention was, and it's very, very clearly stated, repeatedly, repeatedly stated in your evidence-in-chief, that you wanted to go to Jagodnja and Joseva to defend Jagodnja and Joseva; right?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So we are crystal clear about that.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, this might be an appropriate moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, we will have a 25-minute break starting from now. How are you proceeding? MR. DI FAZIO: I'll perform more surgery during the break.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm going to take, as predicted, a goodly part of today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I want to make sure because what I want to ensure is that we are proceeding -- you are proceeding more or less according to what you had planned. MR. DI FAZIO: I think I'll finish, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We'll reconvene in 25 minutes' time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Wubben standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Just a short response by Prosecution related to the motion filed yesterday by the Defence. We will oppose it and we will file within a couple of days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. As early as possible because I think that witness is in the pipeline. All right. So if you can respond within two days, please, we are not going to issue an order shortening the time, but I take it as a commitment on your part that you will file within the couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you have any plan before you got to Jagodnja and Joseva on what to do, what role you were going to play, in the defence of those villages?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you know if you would be able to play any role, that you would be actually able to do anything, to assist in the defence of those villages?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't know anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You said in evidence that when you got there -- yes, when you got there, you found the presence of other groups. I'll just read it briefly -- your evidence to you from the 9th of September, page 6. You were asked: "Did you remain in Jagodnja?" And you answered: "No. Other groups had reached Jagodnja before us from Miholjevine, Mosici, a group from Jagodnja ... the group that was there. They were chasing the Serbs, actually, and shooting after them. And that's how they managed to chase away the Serbs who had come into their village and torched it." So we had in Joseva and Jagodnja on that day the group from Osmace, the group from Kragljivoda, a group from Jagodnja itself, of course, the group from the village, I suppose, and a group from Mosici. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How did these groups come to be concentrated in that area? I mean, we've heard about you, of course, and I suppose Jagodnja, we know that they are based in the village of Jagodnja, but what about the other two, Miholjevine and Mosici? How did they find themselves there at the scene, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The optical visibility of those villages, Miholjevine, Mosici, Mehmedovici, they could optically see what was happening in Jagodnja and Joseva, and as soon as they saw that there was burning, they set off in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So did burning act as a type of attractant or lure to these self-organised groups? Wherever they saw burning, that's where they went? Or did this happen just on this one occasion?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that burning, shooting, everything they could see that, because when it's quiet, when there is no shooting from the village, and then as soon as they are attacked, optically -- there is optical visibility, they defend themselves, as soon as there is burning, they go in that direction, and then those groups go up there, groups that are able to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And was that the -- is that what in fact happened throughout 1992 and early 1993? The Serbs would attack somewhere, somewhere in the Srebrenica area, there would be burning, and whatever group could see the burning would then go to that area? Is that your evidence? As far as you know.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not my evidence. The majority of the villages could not help each other, and those who couldn't help, you know, what could Lijesce, Skelani or Resavici help? They couldn't help Skelani. They were powerless themselves, so what could they do as a rule?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. In your experience in 1992 and early 1993, whenever you were in a place at which groups had converged, different groups, different self-organised groups, had converged, they did so whenever possible because of the sight of smoke. That's what got them there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I don't think this witness can sensibly give evidence or be asked to give evidence in this general way covering a two-year period, or covering 1992 and early 1993, whenever he was in different places, where groups had converged it was because of smoke. I mean, it's such a general question. I mean, unless he's actually asked about specific incidents, he's bound to give an answer which is then going to be pounced upon as unclear or too general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough. Thank you, Mr. Jones. I think you need to rephrase your question, Mr. Di Fazio, limiting it only to -- based on his experience and his knowledge. What would be the general practice, the norm. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, yes, I entirely agree. And that was my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Otherwise, the question as you put it was indeed, as Mr. Jones points out, very generic. MR. DI FAZIO: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Make it clear that you were asking him, limiting only to what he personally knows to be the general practice. MR. DI FAZIO: I entirely agree. My point was -- I had asked that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. but I'll do it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In your experience, I'm talking about your experience, not anyone else, okay, on the basis of what you saw and observed and heard of in 1992 and the early part of 1993, whenever these self-organised groups converged on a particular action, for example, the one you've just been talking about, Jagodnja and Joseva, were they -- did they go there on the basis of seeing burning following a Serb attack?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They didn't as a rule go where -- there was the physical contact of the territory of Muslim villages so that they could help each other, then they would help each other. I'm -- I said several times that there was the case of Muslim villages burning and then it was not possible to help them. Where there was some minimal physical contact, certain groups would go there to help each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. But your convergence on this particular occasion, to Jagodnja and Joseva, your going there in your grouping, self-organised grouping of Osmace men, that wasn't because of burning that you could see, that was because someone had come and called, the villages had come and sought assistance; correct?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's humane to help a person when they are in trouble. We went there. Civilians asked us to help. There wasn't an order. No person arrived. We saw women with children fleeing, leaving the villages. They told us what happened. And then we went to -- we went because of our own humanity, in order to help that particular place that was burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How many groups -- turn to another scene of action for just a moment, if we could. How many groups turned up in Kravica in the period of time that you were there? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Avdagina Njive-Kajici direction, there was my group and the Miholjevine group, which came before we did to the Glogova area. And that's where it joined us there, at Glogova. It didn't come together with us but it joined us later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. I just remind you of your evidence regarding Kravica that you gave on the 9th of September, page 55. I'll read it out to you so that -- we entered Kravica on the 7th of January -- this is an answer: We entered Kravica on the 7th of January, between 10.00 and 11.00 on the 7th of January. Question: How many were in your group? Answer: There were about 50 lads in my group. And during the night, we were joined by lads from Miholjevine -- I can't tell. I think it's Mocici, Delici, led by someone called Zis. Some people from Zanjevo, this group from Osmace, Jagodnja and Joseva. These different groups, and not to mention of course the presence of Ejub Golic's group itself in that area already. Now, how did they all find their way to Kravica at the same time, or at about that time?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either I didn't get the proper interpretation or I didn't understand properly. I just wanted to say between 40 and 50, there were in our group, and how they -- I said group, I mentioned a group, I mentioned Jagodnja, Joseva, Miholjevine, that's one group, and I don't know how that group came and that group joined us in the region. And Ejub Golic was not in the area. This is his village that he held throughout the war period. He was in Glogova. You know, and it was cut off from that village towards Bratunac, so not in the area. He was in his village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Look, Mr. Buric, all I'm saying is that -- I put it to you that the portion of evidence that I just read out to you when you were talking about Kravica indicates that different groups converged to carry out action in those -- that period of time, early January, 7th, 8th and even before, around Kravica.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can talk about my unit only which came to that area around the 5th. We came to help Ejub Golic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question basically is do you have an explanation, how come that all these groups, including your own, all happened to converge in the area to help Ejub Golic more or less at the same time or at least on the same day or day and a half or two days? Do you have an explanation for that? If you have, you have. If you don't have, you don't have.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I don't have an explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's clear. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Let me suggest an explanation to you. I suggest that these groups all converged in places like Jagodnja and Joseva and Kravica, these disparate groups, because there was a central command structure, a central command structure of which you're aware and a central command structure who was headed at the top by Mr. Oric. Would you agree or not with that proposition?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would not agree with that in the least. That is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And that's your right to disagree. That's okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I know what -- how it was out in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Fair enough, fair enough. I'm just putting to you what I -- what I suggest is the case. All right. Now, you have told us that -- and you're absolutely certain about this -- that the purpose in your going to Jagodnja and Joseva in the first place was to assist the people there, but it's your evidence - in fact, I just read it out to you a moment ago - that when you got there, the other groups that had reached Jagodnja before you had managed to chase away the Serbs who had come into their village. So you must agree with me -- you would agree with me that the purpose that you had in moving through dangerous, mined territory, from Osmace all the way up to Jagodnja and Joseva, had vanished by the time you got there. There was no longer any need to help, at least in a military action, up there. That's so, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is not so. I said that those groups that came before that, these were villages which had physical contacts with each other, meaning they were three or four kilometres apart. They touch on each other. Nobody came intentionally from those places. There was no gathering, no convergence, no agreement. It was all spontaneous because Muslim villages were burning, Muslim villages were burning and it was necessary to help those people. Nobody ordered. Nobody was preparing this for days. Yes, let's go to Jagodnja. What it means is that the village is burning, it started burning two hours ago, and those people had to be helped. That was the only reason to go to Jagodnja or Joseva.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Your evidence-in-chief you said the villagers came down from Jagodnja and Joseva and they told you how the Serbs had come into the village and captured some people. You gave evidence about that. And that they -- and you said that they -- there had been fighting with the Serbs entering the village. In fact, I think you said that they -- the Serbs from Fakovici had gone into Jagodnja and Joseva. That's what was reported to you. Fair enough? Is that a fair comment of what you said?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. And you went up to defend Jagodnja and Joseva; correct? That was your only -- that was the purpose?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When you got up there, you found that the Serbs had been chased away; correct?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those units, those groups from Jagodnja and Joseva, as well as Miholjevine and Mosici, they fought the Serbs inside the village and they forced them to retreat towards Fakovici, Boljevici, so the villages of the Fakovici region.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: That's what you said and you just said it again. Now, that means, therefore, doesn't it, that your purpose to defend Jagodnja and Joseva, that was gone. There was no longer any reason for you to be there. My question, therefore, is why did you remain in the area?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We remained because there was shooting non-stop. There was no straight line in the field by which you could tell the Serb side from the Muslim. The Serbs continued shooting, shelling, with all the weaponry they had. It wasn't cut off and there was no point where you could say this area was Serb and that area was Muslim. That was simply the reality in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Just let me remind you of another portion of your evidence that you gave on the 9th of September. Mr. Jones asked you about tanks that were pulling up. And you answered: "When we got to Joseva, a group from Joseva had already pushed Serbs away into the direction of Radijevici, and Sefik and myself, with our ... groups ... went in the direction of Radijevici." So there might have been shooting, there might have been artillery fire, but isn't it the case on your own evidence that the main purpose for you going to this place, Joseva and Jagodnja, had evaporated?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. What evaporated? What reason?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The reason no longer existed. The reason that the villagers had come down and sought your assistance to help with the attack on Joseva and Jagodnja, the capturing of the prisoners, and the defence of those two Muslim villages. When you got there, no such reason existed because they had -- the Serbs had been pushed out, pushed away, into the direction of Radijevici. So the reason no longer existed, did it? The reason you went there in the first place.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were firing so there was some reason. The same one that we came for. There were groups that used infantry weapons and artillery. We followed them because had we returned, they would have continued attacking, so we chased those groups that were still offering resistance. It wasn't a soccer match. It was war. So we followed those groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. So you were chasing the Serbs? Is that what you say? Do I understand you correctly? Chasing the Serbs as they were being -- from Jagodnja and Joseva into the direction of Radijevici?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Who made the decision to switch to the offensive and chase the Serbs back in that direction?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one was making decisions. There was shooting in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
