utterances.text: These were -- movement in -- back then in this area, Mr. Buric, was a matter of life and death, as was illustrated to you on that day because Sefik Mandzic stepped on a mine and blew himself to pieces and other men. Correct? Decisions as to whether or not to chase Serbs to Radijevici, to switch from defending a village to actually an offensive operation to chase Serbs were not light decisions, were they? You just couldn't make a decision like that lightly. You'd have to agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one made the decision. As I said, we followed those groups. We weren't aware as to where we were going in the field. Had we known that there were, say, minefields, that a person would be killed, we wouldn't have gone there. It was a forested area and you didn't know what belonged to who, and there was shooting from both sides. We followed those Serb units and that was the only reason there was. There were constantly shooting. We had some killed and wounded on our part. That was the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So you moved through the forest towards Radijevici and then your evidence is that you continued -- I don't know which way but you certainly continued on towards Fakovici. Why?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Sefik and another two men were killed, my group supposed that to the right there were mines and anti-aircraft machine-guns and guns were firing from the village of Radijevici which is closer to Joseva. That was closer to Joseva than Radijevici. And we stayed to the left close to the creek. So we went to the left, and we came out to the Muslim village of Zanjevo which is to the left of Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: That basically accords with what you've already told us but it doesn't really answer my question. Why did you go towards Fakovici? What was your intention as you were going along this creek in between the villages?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no intention. We saw that to the right there were mines and that there was shooting there and that we couldn't approach the Serbs that way, to the side from which they were firing. That's why we used the creek and went to the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: That might have been why you used the creek and went to the left. But why did you go to Fakovici, in the direction of Fakovici? We know that you ended up there, but why? Why did you go there?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have any sort of intention. It was incidental. It was a natural thing to do. We followed the creek to the left, we didn't have a particular aim, to approach Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Well, you -- you didn't have any aim and you incidentally fought your way into Fakovici. Is that a fair assessment of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And your entry into Fakovici was fairly, according to you, from -- from your evidence, a fairly torrid sort of episode. There was relentless shooting as you approached Fakovici; correct?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You were being fired on before you even got into Fakovici, and as you entered Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were fired on throughout, from Joseva and Jagodnja, all the time, all the way up to Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And in Fakovici, the fighting was hard. You described Serb resistance coming from behind each of the salas [phoen], which I think are barns, in Fakovici, and you described how you had to use Zoljas to take out the five or six Serb soldiers whose bodies you later saw. Do you remember all of that evidence?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Incidentally, you also said in your evidence that -- that in Kravica there was no significant resistance -- on the 9th of September, page 62: "... there was no significant resistance, because ... they were celebrating. Because we found food, lambs on the spit, pigs, ... caught them by surprise, until we reached the centre of Kravica. By that time they ... realised what was happening and they returned fire from everything they had." Yes, it's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You got the date wrong. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm talking about Kravica, the 7th of January. And they had to exit towards Polom and Zelinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So what is the situation? Did you actually have to fight your way into Fakovici or did you catch them by surprise as they were feasting?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, it's bound to be confusing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I agree with you. MR. DI FAZIO: It's my fault entirely and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But it's easy to apologise. Just repeat everything and get the places and the dates right, please. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Buric. My question is: What is the situation? Did you have to fight your way into Kravica -- I'm doing it again -- into Fakovici or did you find them feasting? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I withdraw my question. I think I've misled the witness on this particular -- on this particular portion of evidence, if Your Honours please, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you need a break, Mr. Di Fazio? MR. DI FAZIO: No, just let me gather my -- yes. I think I see now what I've done.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Anyway, the fact of the matter is you had to fight your way into Fakovici; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, is it Fakovici or Kravica that we are talking about? MR. DI FAZIO: Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you want to talk about Fakovici, stick to Fakovici. But -- all right? Go ahead. But make up also your mind what period of time you were talking about, especially if you're thinking about feasting and all that. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. That part was wrong. That's completely wrong and I'll withdraw that. I'm talking about Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you want to stick to Fakovici, stick to Fakovici. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: We're talking about Fakovici, your approach through Radijevici along the creek and into Fakovici, okay? Now, on that particular day did you encounter resistance as you were going into Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the time that we were moving from the direction of Jagodnja and Joseva, they were firing from all directions. From the right side from Radijevici, Kutijesevi, Boljevici, they used mortars and anti-aircraft machine-guns. And from the left side they used the three- and four-barrelled guns. So it is a depression and we were moving towards the east, and there was a hillside there. They supposed that we were in the forest and they were trying to cover that area, firing non-stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. But what I'm actually interested in is as you're going into , into the little hamlet or village of Fakovici, was there resistance to you?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And fairly relentless, hard fighting to get into the -- into Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were there civilians about?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: That's right. You've -- you with asked questions by Mr. Jones about this episode. And, page 20, on the 9th of September, Mr. Jones asked you: "I want to go back to where we left off, because in fact you haven't described your movements yet in Fakovici. We dealt with what was captured. So I want to go back to your entry into Fakovici. I want to first of all ask you -- first of all ask, whether at that time and that day in Fakovici, whether you saw any civilians, Muslim civilians." And you answer yes.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Before -- "Before we moved in that direction, Joseva, Radijevici, and towards the left, I saw thousands, perhaps ... 5.000 and 10.000 people who have already entered the Muslim village of Zanjevo. So a large number of people was coming back with wheat bags from Fakovici and" -- I don't have it very clear in my transcript. I think it's a place called Ambarijo [phoen] or something like that. Okay. Thank you. And: "There were masses of civilians, women and men. In my estimate, between 5 to 10.000 people. And when I was returning, I believe there were ... 15.000." And then to be clear, Mr. Jones says: "All right. You've mentioned they were coming back with wheat bags. It may be an obvious question, but why were the civilians in Fakovici, to your knowledge?" And then you said: "When I was going there, I said from the Muslim of -- the village of Zanjevo. First we went to the left of Zanjevo, and they have already been coming in, looking for food, wheat, corn, whatever they could find, and ... they were returning towards Jagodnja and Joseva." So bearing in mind what you've said of seeing this vast mass of civilians coming back from Fakovici, am I correct that they were already in Fakovici collecting their food, the wheat bags and so on, as you were fighting your way into Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't mention Fakovici. That is not correct. I said they were returning from Muslim village of Zanjevo. A large number of civilians moved when we forced the Serbs to withdraw. And they came from Miholjevina, Mosici, Delici. They followed us, and since the Muslim village of Zanjevo was in between, they entered the Muslim houses there to collect corn and wheat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. I can only go on what is in the transcript. I just -- I won't dwell long on this, but you were asked whether on that day in Fakovici you saw civilians, Muslim civilians, and you said yes, before we moved in that direction, you saw thousands, and then you confined it to Joseva and Radijevici. But then you said: "So a large number of people were coming back with wheat bags from Fakovici." Now, is that just a slip of the tongue? Or is it the case that you --

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what there is in the transcript, but I said the following: I saw people from the Muslim village -- in the Muslim village of Zanjevo and not in Fakovici or Radijevici. So people were returning from the Muslim [as interpreted] of Zanjevo. That village was attacked by Serbs in May 1992 and they were turning towards Jagodnja and Joseva.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Well, we'll leave that topic. You also described the weaponry that you say was seized in Fakovici and you gave detailed descriptions of that. I'm not going to take you through that. But you recall giving that evidence, don't you?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be shown D740?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. You see this -- this document, confidential, Bratunac Brigade document. Yes, sorry, Bratunac garrison command document which is sent to the Birac Brigade command, lists the sort of weaponry that they, the Serbs, seem to think was captured in Fakovici. Now, in your evidence you testified very clearly that when looking at this document, that the Serbs had seized five to six times more weaponry than is listed here. Do you remember that evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Serbs or the Muslims? MR. DI FAZIO: Sorry, the Muslims, I'm sorry, the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you remember that evidence?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You would agree with me, wouldn't you, that the Serbs therefore have made a massive miscalculation in the amount of weaponry they lost?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I'd just object to that question because it presumes that this purports to be an exhaustive list of what was captured. It doesn't say this and only this was captured. Some items are mentioned, so I don't think it can be presumed that it purports to be exhaustive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So limit your question, please, Mr. Di Fazio, to this particular document. MR. DI FAZIO: It's just on the face of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And the face of this document you say it's clearly wrong because a lot more material was in fact recovered, military equipment, was recovered by the Muslim self-organised groups; correct?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We seized more weaponry than what can be found on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: A lot more, a lot more, five to six times more. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I said that, I had ammunition in mind. They didn't mention ammunition here, and as far as I can remember, we took away two tractor loads of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Thank you. I've done with D740. All right. So that list that I just showed you is inaccurate and you've told us that five to six times more was seized. Who did that weaponry go to?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that the list was incorrect. But I said that what is on the list had been seized, plus whatever there was they didn't mention. Most of that weaponry went to Kragljivoda, Jagodnja and Joseva.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And it wasn't just weaponry, but it was also I think a -- significantly two tractor loads of ammunition as well?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tractors.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And who made the decision -- who made the decision that it was to go to Kragljivoda, Jagodnja and Joseva and in what proportions? Who made that decision?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one made that decision. Whatever was seized would be given to an area that had priorities because those Muslim villages were exposed to daily shellings and attacks. And they were the only source of ammunition and weaponry for the Muslims. There was no particular distribution but it went to Jagodnja and Joseva.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: That makes excellent sense, doesn't it, to -- if you get a large amount of weaponry and ammunition, and you're surrounded by a well-armed, ruthless enemy, and you don't have much weaponry and ammunition, then it really makes good sense to be able to prioritise which of the self-organised groups should get weaponry and what proportions. Don't you agree?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree. It wasn't a lot of ammunition or weaponry. It would be a day's worth of ammunition of what was needed for Kragljivoda, Jagodnja and Joseva. It wasn't a lot in the end. So since they received entire convoys, this was just a small chunk.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You mentioned priorities. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes, you said whatever was seized would be given to an area that had priorities. Whatever was seized would be given to an area that had priorities. How were those priorities worked out so that an intelligent, rational decision could be made?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No decision was made. Kragljivoda was the first village closest to the Serbs on the front line, and it was exposed daily to combat activities. As well as Jagodnja and Joseva on the other side. So on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. That might be so but you said, it's your words. The Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. apportionment was based on an area that had priorities. Now, --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically let me try and shorten the debate on this. What Mr. Di Fazio is interested to know from you is who actually decided that it would be Kragljivoda, Jagodnja and Joseva that would take or share amongst them the ammunition and the weapons, and not some other unit or some other place? Because these decisions had to be taken on the spot. So who took these decisions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It all was spontaneous. There were no decisions. All the groups were there and then they would take those weapons and that ammunition, and we were aware that they were more in need of it and that's how it was in those areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I would assume that there would have been some kind of discussion amongst the various groups or the various leaders or -- nothing. Just answer, because I saw you make a gesture with your mouth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no discussion. There was no discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So discussion. So it was a spontaneous thing. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was it the case that different territorial groupings had different military needs, depending on the amount of weaponry they had, the amount of ammunition? For example, someone in Suceska might have needed a lot more ammunition, but another grouping in another part of the Srebrenica area might have needed more guns but not so much ammunition? Did that sort of scenario ever arise as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know one thing: We never participated in anything anywhere close to Suceska, nor did Suceska take part in anything near us. We had no idea what they had, what they were capturing, what they were receiving. I can state with a great degree of certainty what happened with the Osmace group. Osmace is seven kilometres from Kragljivoda. That line, that forest, Kragljivoda, so whatever bullets we had, because we knew that Kragljivoda needed it, so we would give it to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: But again, that was entirely a decision to be made by people in Osmace as to whether or not the people in Kragljivoda would get any of the ammunition or weapons?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I said there was no decision. It was spontaneous. They took it spontaneously or you would just give it on the road, spontaneously when it was found out -- it wasn't found out all immediately. It would take days, perhaps the civilians collected more, women maybe found more ammunition on that day or something like that. So this all turned out spontaneously. There was no decision, no counselling. It was all spontaneous. If something was given up there, what do I know how it was? Who is going to carry for 30 or 40 kilometres? I mean, it's hard to carry five kilogrammes at that distance, never mind to carry a case of ammunition. It wasn't like that out in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's the case of moving to something different. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Let's just ask you very briefly about damage to Fakovici, and I just want to remind you of your evidence. You said 99 per cent of the houses destroyed in Fakovici were destroyed by Serb shelling and not a single house was set on fire. Do you remember that evidence?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that when I returned the next day, the next day meaning on the 6th of October in the morning hours, when I was there, what I saw, meaning that was the only time that I was in Fakovici, that 90 per cent of the devastation was a result of Serb tanks and the fighting that was conducted there in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And were you there I think over a two-day period on -- correct?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Meaning I said that I said that I withdrew at around 3.00 or 4.00 on the 5th, and then I came back in the morning to collect the dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. So one thing the Trial Chamber can be absolutely certain about is that in the course of your group entering and fighting in Fakovici, in the course of the fighting that took place in Fakovici, it wasn't ever necessary for you and your men from Osmace to burn or destroy Serb houses and buildings? That's absolutely crystal clear, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can just say, Your Honours, something that perhaps you don't know, but it's -- it's true for sure. My group, Osmace group, never set one single barn on fire, never mind a house. In the territory of the Srebrenica municipality, there were about 20 churches. Not a single church was damaged. Just allow me to finish. There were 80 mosques, and the Serbs burnt all of them. They razed them all to the ground. Not burned them. They brought bulldozers and burned them. 80 imams were killed in Srebrenica. Not a single Christian priest was killed. Not only -- I mean, we had the chance to burn these facilities but we never did. All the burnings, 99 per cent of the property that wasn't burned in fighting was burned by civilians. The army had no need for that, because after two or three hours they withdrew from that zone, from that area and it was left to the civilians to come back there over days and months to get food.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: That might be so. But in Fakovici, the destruction that you saw and observed was entirely caused by -- almost entirely caused by Serb artillery, Serb tanks firing from across the river, and I think you also said an APC and so on, right? I see you nodding. I take it that's agreement. If you could just speak. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Let's move from Fakovici to Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one clarification for the transcript while Mr. Di Fazio moves to a second question. What the witness said, and it concerned leaving the area. He said, as far as I understood him, that after two or three hours, they withdrew and left that area and then civilians would come for days after that. However, as it states here, on line 11, in the transcript, you could say that they withdrew and that it was left to the civilians, meaning the army left it to the civilians. So could the witness please clarify that part? Could he tell us exactly what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I said exactly was that the army withdrew after two or three hours, meaning that they never came back there again, and that civilians would go back there day after day for days, so individuals, groups, I don't know what kind of civilians went there, but nobody left anything to them. We, these armed groups, withdrew, and then the civilians, without asking anyone, would go back there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Madam Vidovic. That was important because the transcript could -- actually meant something different. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Just one more clarification from your last answer. When you said that the army withdrew, I assume that was a slip of the tongue and what you really meant was the self-organised groups withdrew. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, as you said, army, but I said the armed groups withdrew, meaning that I at no point in my testimony said army or soldiers, but it's as you say, we had armed groups in our terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, let's go to Kravica. You said that Ejub Golic had cut the road between -- between Kravica and Bratunac, right?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And that disrupted communications for the Serbs, didn't it? Because they were --

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: They were based in Kravica and also had a presence in Bratunac, and if that road was cut, that impeded communications between those two Serb areas; correct?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And a gentleman named Kadir Music, I think his name is, told you -- came to see you and told you that the communication line had been cut; correct?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said I'm not sure that his name is Music. Kadir Music or Hamidovic. This can go into the transcript. Hamidovic. Music or Hamidovic is his last name and he came to us at Osmace. He was sent by Ejub, that he entered his own village, meaning all the time that's what we are talking about. Glogova is a purely Muslim village of 700 houses, meaning 700 houses, which was burned in May, the early part of May, 7th, 8th or 9th of May, it was burnt. They held the northern part of Glogova the entire time, and Ejub went to his village, to the western part of the village, and that's where he cut the Bratunac-Kravica communication, where they would use that road every day, received weapons, food, logistics. And then on the other side, the northern side, or the western side, you had the Muslim settlement or village of Konjevic Polje. That's Kravica was very important, actually that Bratunac-Kravica road was very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Right. I want to ask you about decisions again. I'm sorry to keep harping on about it but I'm interested in the process. Who decided that Ejub Golic's request would be entertained and that you would -- that men would be sent from Osmace up to that area?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, Mirsad Dudic was the person in charge in our group. We gathered there. He was -- Kadir was there, and he told us what was being done, and since he could not resist the attacks every day, Ejub, could we then go and help Ejub Golic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that. That was the request. That's what this man came down to speak to you about. And Dudic was in charge. Do I take it that Dudic made the decision, Okay, we are going to go?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't make the decision. He proposed it. We all of us heard it. There were about, I don't know, in Osmace, about 70 or 80 of us that were there on the spot, and he said, who wanted to go? Volunteers? And volunteers volunteered in that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: About how many volunteers?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying about approximately 40 or 50 lads maybe. I don't know, 40 or 50. I don't exactly remember the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All armed or not?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Perhaps half, about 20 of us had arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What did the other unarmed men intend to do? How were they going to be of any use?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what use they were going to be. Perhaps if they captured a rifle, then you could give it to someone or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. The leaving this group in Osmace -- I withdraw the question. By making the decision to leave Osmace and going up to Glogova, the result was that Osmace was left undefended. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned that Osmace is seven kilometres from Kragljivoda, meaning that line was seven kilometres from Osmace.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. But it -- the effect of this group from Osmace going up to operate in the north around Glogova meant that Osmace was left either undefended or the lines were significantly weakened, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no lines at Osmace, meaning there were some 30 men left in Osmace, 30 or 40, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The decision to take the group from Osmace up to Glogova meant that the Glogova -- the Osmace area was -- the defence of the Osmace area was weakened. Correct or not?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, Osmace was not on the front lines and it wasn't weakened. It was inside the territory. Kragljivoda was at the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did the people from Osmace play any role in helping or defending the front line at Kragljivoda?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not every day, because we went when there was need for it at Kragljivoda, when there was a fierce attack always a group of volunteers would go, meaning August, September, October, right until the 23rd of March, 1993. It would be helping Kragljivoda.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Would it have been safer for the inhabitants or the people who were in Osmace in December of 1992 for your armed group to stay in Osmace? Would it have been better and safer for those people, the women and children, the refugees, who were gathered in Osmace?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been better, but we weren't thinking like that. The thinking was different, because in Glogova, as we know, hundreds were killed. There were burnings, people were captured. All that they had was destroyed. So we were primarily there to defend the Muslim property. People had entered their houses. They didn't have any where to live. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. They were dying of hunger, poverty. So in all of that, people had decided to return to their own homes, meaning we were helping people to survive. We are speaking about the struggle to survive in our own homestead. Well, if they don't have a right to do that, then I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you have any idea what your role was to be before you went to Glogova?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The request had come, had been transferred to you, from Ejub Golic. In other words, the man that came to see you said, This is a request from Ejub Golic and his self-organised group. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't request for help. He asked for it. It was an appeal for a person in trouble for help.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Sure. The appeal for assistance to deal with their troubles came from Ejub Golic and his self-organised group; correct?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kadir came to us, said that he was sent by Ejub Golic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Okay. And you went up to the Glogova area, but you didn't speak to Ejub Golic, did you?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went there, but we did not speak with Ejub Golic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You just said, "We did not speak to Ejub Golic." Do I take it that not only did you personally not speak to Ejub Golic but no one in your group spoke to Ejub Golic?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody from our group, because we had Kadir and he showed us where we were supposed to be, because Ejub was completely on the other side, some six or seven kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. So what was the plan when you got there? What -- what were you told to do?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were supposed to defend Glogova from the Kravica and Kajici direction. There were daily attacks from those directions, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thanks. That's all I need to know. Didn't you consider or men in your self-organised group consider it appropriate to go and speak to Mr. Ejub Golic or at least make some sort of -- communicate with him in some way?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because we had Kadir, who took us precisely to the western part of Glogova. We didn't have any need because in the direction where Ejub Golic was, daily or hourly attacks were taking place. They were transporters and tanks from the direction of Bratunac. He cut the communication. And the fighting was going on there. You couldn't cross over to the other side. We couldn't get to Ejub.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you know what the purpose of your role was, the role of you -- of your Osmace self-organised group? What precisely its role was?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our role specifically, from what Kadir conveyed to us, was the defence or the guarding of the Kravica-Kajici-Avdagina Njiva communication, to prevent the Serbs from Kravica approaching Ejub from the other side. They would then have to withdraw automatically from those positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you have any contingency plans in the event that your grouping was attacked and forced to retreat or move from the area?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kadir told us -- actually, Kadir showed us the road we could use to withdraw. That's the southern part of Glogova, which we held the whole time. He showed us that direction if the Serbs were to break the lines from Bratunac or Kravica where we could go back, withdraw to the southern part, towards Bljeceva. That part of Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, on this occasion, other groups also arrived to help as well, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That first evening, us -- well, in the morning, we surveyed the Serb lines and the positions and then we told Kadir that we could only see a few men in that direction. I'm talking strictly about asphalt. My group was stationed near the asphalt road, and in that sector we didn't see too many men, since we knew that they had withdrawn, that they had already started drinking and celebrating because they were using a lot of shells. We saw that, and then we sent Kadir to convey further what we saw on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were there other groups operating in the area apart from Osmace, the Osmace grouping, and Ejub's group? Operating in conjunction with you and/or with Ejub, that you're aware of.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning, or actually evening hours, or when it was getting light, we were joined by a group, a group as I said led by a certain Zis. I don't know where it came from, maybe from Bljeceva. That group at our direction, Avdagina Njiva-Kajici-Kravica. That's where that group joined us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And I think there were groups from Miholjevine and Mocici as well, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the group, meaning the person in charge was a certain Mefail, or Zis. Miholjevine, Mocici, yes, that's that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now at any point in time any of these groups could have withdrawn from the area and gone back to their local areas if they had so wished; correct?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They could have. It was all on a voluntary basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. All right. I want to ask you about your entry into Kravica. You -- I think you said that you entered Kravica on the -- sorry, at around 10.00 a.m. Would that be -- does that accord with your memory?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And as you went into Kravica, Kravica, the Serbs started shooting at you with all available means; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So you agree that you had to fight your way into Kravica, and that you did so at some point after 10.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 10.00 and 11.00 a.m., I said there were few men. There were a couple of houses there on that road, the Kajici-Kravica road. There wasn't a lot of resistance there. Up until the approach to Kravica. Right up until the very approach to Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So the fighting started at some point after 10.00 or 11.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fighting lasted for days there. They were firing all the time from all sides, but that was -- they were looking for a moment of weakness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Sure, sure. Now on the 6th you did a reconnaissance of the lines and on the 7th you entered into Kravica; correct?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And they were already underway feasting and drinking and eating; correct?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it was they were doing. But they were firing from all sides, from all weaponry available, and when they withdrew later we saw that food was left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose they were feasting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So it was a surprise attack at about some time about -- sometime after 10.00 or 11.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It appeared so, along that axis [Realtime transcript read in error "exist"]. It was their moment of weakness. And we approached the settlement. We came very close.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Just the time, Mr. Buric. It was sometime after 10.00 or 11.00, you attacked sometime after 10.00 or 11.00; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, it's a matter of the interpretation and the transcript. I mean, it says at line 12, page 68, "along that exist." I know that's probably going to be corrected to "along that axis." But I understood that witness said something more like in that direction, or in that particular part, i.e., that was a surprise attack in that particular area or something of that nature which was said, and I don't think that's going to appear in the final transcript. So we might want to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Jones. Do you confirm that, Mr. Buric? Please say "da" or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was talking about a direction, by the asphalt road that was taken by my group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Look, would you disagree with me if I suggested to you that this was a surprise drawn attack on Kravica?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not a surprise attack. I don't know on what day Ejub entered Glogova precisely but on those days they were using all weaponry and attacking from all directions. Serbs held Avdagina Njive which was a Muslim settlement. We came during their moment of weakness where they had few men. We came in and went along in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So it was not a dawn surprise attack. I'd like you to look, please, at D469. You were shown this document by Mr. Jones during your examination-in-chief, and he took you through the contents of it. I want you to turn to the Serb version, just be -- if we can get through this quickly before the break. You see the words [B/C/S spoken], then a sentence and then a list. I want you to read into the transcript the list beginning with the words [B/C/S spoken].

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of fighting, the 3rd Kravica Infantry Battalion, that included the 3rd Kravica Infantry Battalion, on the 7th of January, 1993, from 6.30 until 2.00 p.m., in the course of withdrawing, the 3rd Infantry Battalion left the following MTS behind in Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment, Mr. Di Fazio. Before we proceed any further. Because again, I need this cleared up. The witness clearly said reading out from this document on the 7th of January, from 6.30 until 2.00 p.m., 6.30 in the morning, I take it. But in the English text that we have it says in the course of combat between the hours of 0830 and 18 hours. So ... MR. DI FAZIO: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, okay. But we need to address this. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you are correct. This is yet another mistranslation. The original Bosnian document states during the fighting, that included the 3rd Kravica Battalion, on the 7th of January, 1993, between 6.30 until 4.00 p.m., during the withdrawal of the 3rd Kravica Infantry Battalion the following MTS was left behind in Kravica. And it was stated that the combat lasted between 8.30 until 6.00 p.m. The document in our language has a different meaning than what was translated into English. Perhaps the witness could comment. So the original doesn't specify that the combat lasted during those hours, but, rather, that the battalion was withdrawing in that time period. Perhaps Mr. Buric could comment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said around -- around 10 hours, that was the direction that was used. We heard shooting from other locations as well. They withdrew in the evening towards the north. Towards Polom and Zelinja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am looking at the B/C/S version and the second line it says 0630 to then 16 hours. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, with respect, it does, it does, and it's plain as a pikestaff. It's absolutely crystal clear, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I know that the whole exercise basically arises from your previous question as to whether he would agree that this was a surprise dawn attack. So please concentrate on that and let's get moving on it. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I'm not going to be long on the topic and then perhaps we'll break.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So having read there document that says that in the course of combat, which the Serbs seem to think started at about 6.30 in the morning and went to 4.00 in -- yes, 4.00 in the afternoon, does -- does that make you think that perhaps you might be wrong about the attack starting at 10.00 or -- sometime later in the morning, and it not being a dawn attack?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't say 9.00. I said approximately between 10.00 and 11.00, in that direction. So I kept insisting on that direction, Avdagina Njive-Kajici-Kravica, the asphalt road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Okay. I think I've gone as far as I need to with this document. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, this would be an appropriate time for the break. Looking at my notes I will finish and I will finish soon after the break, I hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But out of an abundance of precaution, I think Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I will restrict the break to 25 minutes and would appeal to everyone to try and be as punctual as possible. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can I just say one thing? I mean, in case there was any implications that, as Mr. Di Fazio said, it was plain as a pikestaff I think was his expression, what the correct translation should be. This was the Office of Document Management that translated for us, it's not our translation -- I don't want it suggested that we missed something which was blatantly obvious. MR. DI FAZIO: I am not making that suggestion at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. It didn't even cross my mind, actually. Anyway, 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: I just have three --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio, I see they put my name expecting me to say Mr. Di Fazio. Go ahead. MR. DI FAZIO: I have just a very few more questions for you which I'm sure we can whip through fairly quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Firstly, I needn't take you through all the evidence but you gave quite a bit of evidence regarding all the weaponry that was seized in Kravica. You described the place being -- well, I think you said every house had some weapons in it and that you seized a lot of weapons, and you also said that most of the weaponry was given to Biljeg, Glogova and other villages. Was this again just a spontaneous thing as happened in the case of the weaponry seized in Fakovici or was there some sort of decision-making process going on here, as far as this weaponry was concerned?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were no decisions made those guys collected most of that weaponry. In Glogova there was the line, and there was Miholjine, Mosici, the villages there, there were daily attacks there, and we seized a bit of weaponry there. A little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You testified on Thursday last week that none of your men knew how to lay mines in March of 1993. But you -- sorry, I don't want to misquote you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see that -- and the reaction of course would be justified because although we could follow the interpretation of what the witness was saying, his answer did not show up in the transcript. Or only a part of it did. So perhaps you could -- MR. DI FAZIO: In relation to the previous question about the weaponry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. As you see, there is no interpretation and I saw Ms. Vidovic and Mr. Jones -- MR. DI FAZIO: No, no, that's fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- conversing. So I anticipated that myself. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Look, I'm just reminding you about the weaponry. You said that a lot of weapons were seized and that there it was a lot of weaponry in Kravica. And that it was given to Biljeg Glogova and other villages. Was this particular distribution of weapons a spontaneous thing as happened in Fakovici, or was there some other way of deciding who was to receive what weaponry?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no decisions made. It was spontaneous. If you found something, you took it. And there was no distribution or an agreement on it. It was far more spontaneous.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Now, let's turn to mining. You said that none of your men knew how to lay mines in March 1993. Do you remember that evidence?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said throughout the activities in the area of the Srebrenica municipality, in April and March, so April 1992 until March 1993, no one from amongst my group of people knew how to lay mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And that's because it's a -- something that requires a great deal of special training, according to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: However, in Kravica, members of your group, none of whom knew how to lay mines, went in and demined the building, the building of the farmers' cooperative, and it was mined heavily. Where did they acquire the skills to go in and demine this heavily mined building if they didn't know how to do it?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where your information came from. There is one type of mines laid out in the field but this was just dynamite under the building, and one needed a plain lighter to light it. Mines in the field are a completely different thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Well, hang on. You didn't mention any dynamite laid under the building. Let me just remind you precisely of what you said, page 61, on the 9th of September: "I saw on the left, in the centre of Kravica, next to the supermarket, there was a building, I believe a building of the farmers' cooperative, and it was mined. My group went in, and they demined the building and we seized large amounts, and it was mined heavily, and we also seized a lot of weapons." You mentioned mines on three or four occasions in that answer, nothing about dynamite. You were very clearly talking about land-mines, not dynamite, weren't you, when you gave that answer?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are mistaken. Your Honour, if something is being set up an explosive, in Bosnian we say "miniranje." They used industrial dynamite used for bringing down buildings or in mines. So they put dynamite, plate [as interpreted] dynamite with a fuse, and one had to approach it and light it with a lighter or a match. They simply took out the fuse to defuse it. I don't know how much dynamite was there, but it was in at least three to four locations. So these are two different categories. And we use the word of "miniranje" to set up explosives. You mentioned minefields but that's a different category.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How long were the fuses?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for the transcript, which remains unclear, two or three times the witness said "miniranje," and that it has a wider connotation in our language. I -- perhaps the transcript missed that. It does not appear in the transcript, the word "miniranje." So I would kindly ask the witness to confirm whether he mentioned the word of "miniranje."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, "miniranje." It means setting up explosives, dynamite, to mine something. That's what we used in our language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Just to confirm that in the interpretation that I was receiving in my ear phones, I mean, it was mentioned each time the witness mentioned it. So let's proceed. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What's the word for dynamite in your language?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dinamit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Well, why didn't you use the word "dinamit" when you were describing the soldiers who went into the cooperative building in Kravica and plucked out the fuses from the dynamite or dinamit?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it was mined and there was no need for me to say "dinamit." I said the building was mined but not in the sense of laying mines. I meant the word of "miniranje" which has a much wider connotation in our language.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that we may be of assistance in need of spelling out the word for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It can be arranged later on. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Last topic. Just that the destruction that you -- you observed in Kravica, your position is that you -- the destruction that you saw in Kravica was clearly caused by Serb shells fired from Serbian tanks into Kravica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You saw no damage or aware of any damage having been caused by arson or deliberate torching of houses, Serb houses or buildings; correct?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see it during the time I was in that area. I didn't see anything like that. I didn't see torching of houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And once again, it wasn't necessary for you and your fighters in carrying out your combat actions in Kravica, to burn or set fire to Serb houses and buildings; correct?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a moment ago, as part of my evidence and I claim with full responsibility that my group from April 1992 until the end of March of 1993, never set a single Serb barn on fire, let alone a house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. And just lastly, just confirm this for me. It wasn't necessary, was it, for you and your group when carrying out combat fighting operations in Kravica, to burn down houses? I'm not asking if you did it but there was just no reason to do such thing. You were able to carry out your combat actions in Fakovici -- in Kravica without burning down Serb houses or buildings, right?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We conducted an operation, an activity and we didn't set anything on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much for answering my questions, Mr. Buric. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. And also for your efforts to finish in good time to allow for a re-examination and questions from the Bench to come to an end today. Yes, Mr. Buric, there is going to be a short re-examination now from Mr. Jones. Mr. Jones, go ahead. Please leave us about ten minutes maximum.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Buric, firstly I want to start with something you said yesterday. And it's page 43, line 16 to 17 of the transcript. "I never saw Naser or Masic in 1993. The first time I saw Naser was - I don't know - sometime in late March or ... April of 1993." My question is: It follows from that, I take it, that you never saw Naser Oric in Osmace in 1992 or the first three months of 1993?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. And now when you were being asked about the book by Masic, and also the book allegedly by Oric, and it's page 44, lines 23 to 25. You were asked whether Mr. Naser Oric would be in a good position to write a book about events in 1992. And you said: "I wouldn't agree, and I believe ... with 99 per cent certainty that Naser did not even have 80 per cent of the information about what was going on in the Srebrenica region." My question is: Sorry, I shall continue a tiny bit. You said: All the events that would come out later, exaggerated, I don't know, that's something that happened, and I believe that Naser did not have the right or the proper information about what was happening in the territory of the Srebrenica region. I just want to ask you why do you say that? Why do you not believe that Naser Oric had the right or proper information about what was happening in the Srebrenica region?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose rather I claim that he wasn't in the area throughout, in the area of Jagodnja and Joseva, Kragljivoda, Osmace. He never saw those areas. It's a vast area. I said that in May of 1992 over 2.000 houses were set on fire in that area. And another two to two and a half thousand houses later, in March of 1993, and he didn't see that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I have one question which I'd like to put in private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session for a couple of minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask a question which relates to P566, which is the Masic book.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The one complication, Your Honours, is that yesterday you were provided with an extract and you'll recall that one page had a photograph of the witness, and I believe you removed the other page which in fact I want to refer the witness to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's -- we had two separate documents, and I'm not even in the position to confirm that they were both from the same book. We kept that two-page exhibit which has allegedly the photo of Mr. Buric in the Bosnian/Serb version, front page, and the other document was withdrawn by the Prosecution. In other words, they said we don't -- we are not going to make use of it, so we never saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I might have to reintroduce it then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not a problem at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The ERN -- because we might not have copies for everyone now. We can provide copies tomorrow. I have one copy which I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think they might still be available from yesterday; I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's 01099834 is Bosnian. And there's the English. That's one spare copy in any event. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I don't object to new evidence going in as long as it's to clarify a point in the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, let's wait and see. Let's not jump to conclusions. MR. DI FAZIO: I assume that's why it's there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the purpose of trying to reintroduce this document into the records during re-examination? What are you seeking to prove?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it goes to the reliability of this book which was a matter in cross-examination, which was -- it was put to the witness that actually since he hadn't read the book all he could say is that the one small section which I'd showed to him wasn't accurate. This was distributed by the Prosecution, and we noted that there is something else where the witness's name is mentioned and it was in the extract with his photograph, so it seemed that only a matter of one question. I can clarify. MR. DI FAZIO: No problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would expect you to say no problem. But we can make use of this document now, and as soon as you finish with it we give it a number, an exhibit number, and Madam Usher will seek to have it photocopied --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- for everyone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's the section in English, it's under the heading, "organisation of the local authorities and possibilities of defence." And it says in English, there we go: "All activities of the local authorities during the combat activities were done by the War Presidency and the executive authority of Srebrenica municipality, War Presidency, executive board was done by." And then there is a list of names, and the very last name is Nesib Buric. Do you see that, Mr. Buric? Do you see that? I have a question.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it. Yes. I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Simply this: If we read combat activities to refer to the period before demilitarisation, were you actually involved in the activities of local authorities or the activities of the Srebrenica municipality during combat activities?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I went down into Srebrenica - I'm now talking about the April 1992, March 1993 period - was on the 23rd of March, 1993 to the Kragljivoda line, the village of Osmace and so on. So that was the first time I came to Srebrenica. This actually is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That was all. That was simply it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. This will become Defence Exhibit D7 --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D749, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Witness Buric, you were asked some questions about offensive and defensive use of land-mines today, if you recall that. I just want to ask you four questions in that regard and you can provide short answers if possible. You told us how in Fakovici on the 6th of October 1992, the Serbs had mined dead bodies of Muslim civilians. Are you able to say whether that's an offensive or a defensive use of land-mines? Do you see any meaningful distinction there?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that their mines were used as means of combat. They knew we would come to gather the corpses and they were mined, meaning the idea was to destroy as many Muslims as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. You've also told us how the Serbs mined Muslim villages, for example Zanjevo. And you might have mentioned Voljavica as well; I'm not sure. But in any event you said that Muslim villages where the inhabitants had been expelled were nonetheless mined by the Serbs. My question is this: Did the presence of land-mines contribute to the problems of starvation in the enclave? In other words, did they -- did they present an obstacle to people getting food?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Wherever Muslim civilians moved in search of food, the Serbs would lay mines there, and if you were to take a map of the mined areas in Srebrenica, you would find that 80 per cent of the Muslim villages had minefields in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. So if we imagined a situation where you're a group of people surrounded by mines and you have no food and you're not able to go out and get food because of those land-mines, do you see whether that's an offensive or a defensive use of land-mines, if it's a meaningful distinction even?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be the offensive use of land-mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. And finally on this, I don't want to dwell too much, but I don't know if you appreciate it but it was being suggested to you that when Serbs put land-mines around their villages because they were frightened they were cowering in their villages, fearing an attack by a powerful Muslim army, that's the gist -- MR. DI FAZIO: That's exaggerated the point of the evidence. I don't mind Mr. Jones clarifying that but he misstates what I put and the effect of my cross-examination. I agree that it was put as a defensive --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Could you rephrase your question now. In any case, the words have been said now, Mr. Di Fazio. So perhaps you could rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Simply this: When it comes to Serbs laying land-mines around their villages, do you see that as a defensive use of land-mines or is it still in the spirit of the use of -- the offensive use which you've described?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Offensive use.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown P21, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, P21, please, usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you were shown this document and it's simply to ask you this: If we look at this -- this obviously relates to -- to Naser Oric. We see at number 6, active policeman in the Srebrenica SGB, and then at B, it says, corporal, BH army, scout. Now, to your knowledge, was Naser Oric a corporal in the BH army, and did he ever act as a scout?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Would a scout be the same thing as a courier?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. I'll leave that. Thank you very much. P22, please. I'm moving through the exhibits as quickly as I can. You were also shown this document. One point the name at the bottom, Dragan Kovacevic, is that a Serb or Muslim name?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan, I think that's a Serb name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. On this document, do you see any sign that this document was ever received in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 8th Operations Group in 1994 was in Srebrenica, so why would this be received in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. That's fine. Thank you. Now, you were asked about the interview which appeared in Dani, which you spoke to a journalist. You were asked a number of questions about that. I might get that in front of me for a moment. Now, you explained what you meant when you used the expression Naser, and it doesn't say Oric, I note, in the original, but the Naser who honourably led us, and you explained what you meant by that, so I'm not going to dwell on that. I simply want to ask you this: I'm sorry, I'm just going to find the reference. Sorry, Your Honour, in the interests of time -- well, no. There is an expression here where it says, and I think it's attributed to you, "I'm a hundred per cent disabled, a brother of sehid." And then there is a reference to a "sehid" family. Just to clarify that point, can you explain what's meant by that, in particular, is that -- is that anything to do with -- with Mujahedin and martyrs as we've come used to the term in the context of other countries, or does it have some other meaning in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said after I was heavily wounded in the Srebrenica demilitarised zone, I am a hundred per cent disabled person. My brother was killed, meaning, also in the demilitarised zone. The word "sehid" is a Bosnian word which means a person who is killed. A person who is killed, that word, the word to denote this person, is sehid. A person who was killed is a sehid. It's not a Mujahedin term or anything. It's a purely Bosnian word, a word of Bosnian Muslims. The word sehid is used to denote a person who was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. I thought that was worth clarifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd like to ask a couple of questions about P570 and P571. Could the witness be shown those documents. And those are the lists which he was shown purportedly from Osmace and from Biljeg. I think it might help, as the Prosecution did, to have P80 as a comparison. First I want to ask you this: Would you agree that it appears that this document was prepared either with a typewriter or with the aid of a computer? It's not handwritten, in other words.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's either typed or drafted on a computer. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right? MR. DI FAZIO: Which document is the witness looking at? It's just not clear --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: P570 it should be. MR. DI FAZIO: P570, and that's -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In 1992 or early 1993 in Osmace, did you have either computers or a computer or a typewriter?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not a single one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you have electricity?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. You described this document as a census. By that, do you mean a census of the whole population or just the male population? We noted that there are only male names in this list.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably a census of the male population in one village.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. And then when we look at the document which is very similar from Biljeg, you told us the other day how in Biljeg it was a wooded area, you even compared it to the Sehiti camp, or spoke about it in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the same breath. To your knowledge, did they have computers or typewriters in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What? To your knowledge, did they have computers or typewriters in 1992 in Biljeg.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I'm not getting a translation. But no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I think just to be clear for the record he said, yes, confirming the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The answer to your previous question was yes. And I would have found it really difficult to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there were none, no, no. I didn't say yes. I said that there were none.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It was also pointed out to you that many of the people in these lists were of fighting age or military-capable age. Two questions in that regard. Was everyone at the time who was capable of fighting in fact armed with a rifle and actually engaged in fighting?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I said throughout the whole period of resistance, it was all on a voluntary basis. Only those lads who wanted to go on a voluntary basis, there were no lists, nothing to report, to, nothing like that. It was strictly on a voluntary basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, one thing on the Biljeg document. It's right, isn't it, that in Biljeg there were a lot of refugees from Skelani?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, it was suggested to you that there weren't many old people in these lists. Do you know what happened to a large number of the old people, old Muslims, in the Skelani area in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the people that did not manage to flee to the woods were killed in Skelani, Lijesce, Resavici, Dodrak [phoen]. All the people who did not manage to escape were killed. I said the elderly, the retarded, the disabled. They were all killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Now it was pointed out to you that in the P570 Osmace list we have 121 people, a very precise number, and we have 136 people for Biljeg. And then it was pointed out that in P80, those exact same figures appear for Biljeg and for Osmace. I think Osmace company and the Biljeg company. Now, my question is, and only if you can help us, do you think that possibly P80 was based on these documents as the source? In other words, that they are based on the same information rather than independent sources?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why are you asking the witness this question? I mean, it's a submission that you can make at a later stage, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right, okay. That's fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think the witness can help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour. I will make that submission. It's already on the record anyway. If I could show the witness P75 quickly. I am bearing in mind the time. I hope to finish shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because we need more than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact, rather than showing the witness the document I think I can take the point this way: You were shown a document in which it was stated that Atif Krdzic was from Srebrenica and in that context you gave evidence that in fact he had worked in Srebrenica. Before you retired, where were you working?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked at the Brezani elementary school before the war. And, as I said, Atif worked in Srebrenica before the war. And I said clearly that he lived in Osmace and Bratunac, meaning that he worked in Srebrenica and lived at Osmace and Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: To make this point really, after the war, where were you living and working?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the war, in 1993, I lived in Srebrenica as a refugee and an expellee. With the fall of Srebrenica and after my wounding, I lived in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you work in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the Srebrenica municipal office which was formed in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You work in Tuzla. Are you from Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I am from Osmace, and I worked in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, concerning Fakovici, you were asked about documents which were recovered from Fakovici and whether they would have been useful as a matter of intelligence. You told us how you'd captured a certain amount of weapons and ammunition in Fakovici. At that stage, did you actually need information from some other source as to what you had captured or, as far as you were concerned, was that sufficient, you had what you had and didn't need to be told what you had?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were not interested in information at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Is there any way that information -- well, I'll withdraw that question. I want to explore very briefly, because we are short on time, the notion of the voluntariness of fighters in this period in 1992, and you've told us a lot about that. But it was suggested to you that perhaps that it was strange that people might be able to just come and go and leave an action in the midst of it. Now, firstly, or you've told us that actually people did leave the lines on at least one occasion. At the same time, though, people often remained, did they not, in an action even though they could leave? They remained and they fought in the action?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned just once but it happened on several occasions that a part of the volunteers would leave the lines and then come back, as soon as they heard. It wasn't controlled. I mean, somebody may or may not have been able to have any influence on another person.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And simply this: When people did remain, when they did actually fight together, at the risk to their lives, why did they do that rather than simply leaving and going home?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said in -- at the beginning of my testimony that this was a struggle for survival. A man knows -- I mean, he can run wherever he wants to, but his turn will come. And like I said, people went from Kragljivoda to Osmace, from Osmace somewhere else. But then their turn came. It was just a struggle for survival. That was the only thing a person had. Their lives. And they were going to lose that as well. Like I said, in the beginning of my testimony, 12.000 people lost their lives from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. I just have three last questions. For Fakovici, would it be a fair summary of your testimony that there was an attack from Fakovici towards Joseva and Jagodnja and that then you were in pursuit of the Serbs and in fact you pressed the advantage and went into Fakovici? Is that a fair summary of what you were telling us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones, next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
